title: Ang 345–346: Begampura
hook: Ravidas's city without sorrow closes Gauri
tomorrow: why does Asa open with a hymn you may already know?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kabir's alphabet: fifty-two letters, each one pointing past itself. Gauri has one more page, and a different voice gets it.

Every home listing sells the same dream: a quiet street, good schools, low taxes. On ang 345 there's a poem about a perfect city, and here's the odd part. Among the things it doesn't have, it lists taxes. Not only sorrow and fear: taxes, property, a gate that keeps people out. Who puts a tax office into a hymn? The poet signs his name at the end. Ravidas.
screen: `A PERFECT CITY, IN A HYMN.` → `NO SORROW. NO FEAR. NO TAX?` → `WHO WROTE THAT IN?`

segments.voice: Ravidas tells you who he is in the hymn's last line, in paraphrase: says Ravidas, the leatherworker, now set free. His city is Begampura, the city without sorrow. Here it is, in paraphrase: no pain or worry lives there; no anxiety, no tax, no property to guard; no fear, no fault, no dread of falling. There's no second or third rank there; all are one. People go wherever they please, and no one at the palace stops them. Now the puzzle solves itself. Ravidas isn't listing what heaven lacks in general. He's listing what pressed on people like him: the tax collector, the fear, the rank you were born into, the door you weren't let through. His city has none of it. Then he says, in paraphrase, now I have found this fine homeland, and it's well there, always, my brother. Readers differ on what Begampura is: a state of the soul, a city still to be built, or both. The hymn doesn't settle it. It ends with an invitation instead: whoever is a citizen there is my friend. A page later, Gauri closes, its last word given to a welcome.
screen: `RAVIDAS, THE LEATHERWORKER, SET FREE.` · `NO SORROW, NO TAX, NO FEAR.` · `NO SECOND OR THIRD RANK.` · `WHOEVER LIVES THERE IS MY FRIEND.` · then, large: `THE CITY WITHOUT SORROW.`

segments.voice: Read ang 345 slowly if you can. Then look at the nearest door, the front door or the one to this room, for the whole sit. Let it stand for every door that's ever been shut on someone, and rest in Ravidas's picture of a city where it simply opens.
Ang 345. The page of the Guru Granth Sahib where Ravidas names Begampura, the city without sorrow.
Keep this one: the city without sorrow, where nobody is second or third. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Ravidas's Begampura hymn is read in order near the close of Raag Gauri and is also sung as kirtan; Sikhs and the followers of Ravidas both hold his hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib dear.

notes: 2026-10-15 v3 written: shape puzzle (the odd detail: a hymn about a perfect city lists taxes among what it lacks; solved by reading what pressed on people like Ravidas).

Ang 345 Begampura hymn paraphrased line by line: no sorrow or anxiety (dookh andohu), no worry, tax or property (tasvees, khiraaj, maal), no fear, fault or decline (khauf, khataa, taras, javaal), no second or third rank (dom na sem), roam as they please, no one stops them at the palace (mahram mahal na ko atkaavai), 'now I have found this fine homeland' (khoob vatan), signed 'Ravidas the leatherworker, set free' (khalaas chamaaraa). Confirm each sense.
'Chamaar' rendered as 'leatherworker', the trade it names; it is Ravidas's own self-description in the hymn. Keeper to confirm the rendering is respectful and accurate.
'Readers differ' on an inner, social or future Begampura: hedged on purpose; no reader named.
Days 1484 (Kabir's caste question) and 1488 (the light, not caste) sit near this one; today's angle is the city's earthly details, with rank as one item, not the center.
howItsDone says followers of Ravidas also hold his hymns dear: confirm wording is fair to the Ravidassia community.
